body: A hedgehog is a small animal. It has many sharp spines. The spines keep it safe. At night it looks for food. It likes to eat snails and insects. In the day it rests.

title: Friend of the Garden
body: The hedgehog is a night animal that we often meet in gardens and meadows. On its back it has several thousand sharp spines. When it is frightened, it rolls up into a tight ball, so that only the spines are left on the outside. In this way it protects itself from foxes and other attackers. During the day it likes to sleep in the leaves or under a bush, and at night it sets off to find food. It loves snails, worms and insects. In winter, when the cold comes, the hedgehog sleeps so deeply that it wakes up only in spring. We call this winter sleep hibernation.

title: The Night Traveller
body:
The hedgehog is a night animal that we love to see in our gardens. During the day it hides in the leaves or under a bush, and when dusk falls, it sets off to find food. Its nose is very sensitive, so it can smell a worm or a snail even in the dark.

On its back the hedgehog has several thousand sharp spines. When it senses danger, it tightens its muscles and rolls up into a tight ball. Only the spines are left on the outside, while its soft tummy stays safely hidden. Hardly anyone dares to touch such a prickly ball.

When winter draws near, the hedgehog finds a warm hiding place and falls fast asleep. Its heart beats more slowly, its body cools down, and so it uses very little energy through the cold months. It wakes up only in spring, when the warmer sun begins to shine.

title: A Hedgehog's Year
body:
The hedgehog is one of the best-loved animals in our gardens, though we rarely see it in daylight, since it lives at night. Its back is covered with a suit of armour made of several thousand sharp spines. These spines are not poisonous and they do not shoot out, as some fairy tales claim — the hedgehog uses them only to defend itself. When it senses danger, it tightens the muscles on its back and in an instant rolls into a tight ball. Only a forest of spines is left outside, while its soft tummy stays safely hidden. Few attackers dare such a prickly ball.

The hedgehog is a useful friend to gardeners, because it feeds on snails, worms, insects and other small creatures that would nibble the plants. At night it travels surprisingly long distances, and its sensitive little snout helps it track down even hidden food.

When winter draws near and the nights turn bitterly cold, the hedgehog prepares for a long rest. In the leaves or under a bush it weaves a warm nest, curls up and falls fast asleep. Its heart beats more slowly, its body cools, and it uses only a little energy all winter. Only when the spring sun shines again does the hedgehog wake, stretch, and set off again on its night-time travels.

title: How a Dolphin Sees with Sound
body:
The dolphin is one of the cleverest animals in the world. It lives in the sea and swims beautifully, yet it is not a fish — it is a mammal, like a dog, a horse or a person. That is why it cannot breathe under water. It takes in air through a hole on top of its head and must often swim up to the surface.

Dolphins find their way with sound. They send out quick clicks, which bounce off fish and rocks and come back again. From the echo the dolphin works out where food is and what lies ahead. We call this echolocation.

Although it spends its whole life in the sea and swims faster than many a fish, it is not a fish itself — it is a mammal, just like a dog, an elephant or a person. That is why it cannot breathe under water. It takes in air through a breathing hole on top of its head, so every few minutes it must return to the surface.

They talk together with whistles, clicks and squeaks. Each dolphin even has its own special whistle, by which its friends recognise it — a kind of name it carries all its life.

Most amazing of all is their ability to see with sound. A dolphin sends out quick clicks that travel through the water. When the sound hits a fish, a rock or a sunken ship, it bounces back. From this echo the dolphin works out exactly how far away something is and how big it is — even in complete darkness or muddy water. We call this skill echolocation, and it helps the dolphin find food and stay clear of danger.

title: The Bird That Swims
body:
A penguin is a bird that cannot fly. Its wings have turned into strong flippers, so it is a true master of swimming. Under the water it moves so fast and so smoothly that it looks as if it is flying — only it flies through the sea.

Most penguins live in the cold south, where everything is full of ice and snow. A thick layer of fat and dense, smooth feathers keep them warm. When it is really cold, penguins press together into a big huddle and warm one another.

On land they walk slowly and waddle from side to side. On the ice they often throw themselves onto their tummies and slide, which looks very funny. Parents care for their chicks together and keep them warm under their own warm tummies.

title: The Giant of the Deep
body:
The whale is the largest animal that lives on our planet. The blue whale, the biggest of all whales, can be longer than three buses and heavier than about thirty elephants. Despite its giant size, the whale is a gentle animal that feeds on tiny sea creatures.

Although it spends its whole life in the sea, the whale is not a fish but a mammal — like a dolphin or a person. That is why it must breathe air. When it comes to the surface, it blows a great spout of water and air out of a hole on its back, high into the sky. Sailors recognise a whale by this spout from far away.

Some whales talk to one another with deep sounds that we call singing. Their song travels through the water so far that another whale, hundreds of kilometres away, can hear it. Scientists think they tell each other in this way where they are and where there is food.

Whales live for a long time. Some reach more than a hundred years. Every year they travel huge distances — in summer they swim to cold seas rich in food, and in winter they return to warmer waters, where their young are born.

title: The Bat Hunts in the Dark
body:
The bat is the only animal with wings that truly flies and yet is not a bird, but a mammal. Its wings are not covered with feathers but with thin skin, stretched between its long fingers.

Most bats sleep during the day and set off to hunt at dusk. They hang upside down in caves, in attics or in holes in trees. When darkness falls, they fly out and hunt insects, among them mosquitoes.

The most unusual thing is how a bat finds its way in the dark. It makes sounds so high that our ears cannot hear them. These bounce off obstacles and insects and come back again. From the echo the bat knows exactly where its food is and where it must fly. That is why, even in complete darkness, it never bumps into anything.

title: The Brown Bear and the Long Winter
body:
The brown bear is the biggest predator in our woods. Despite its giant size and sharp claws, it likes best of all to feed on plants. It eats huge amounts of berries, mushrooms, roots and honey, and now and then it catches a fish or a smaller animal too. It is because of its love of sweet honey that it got its name.

The bear has an outstanding sense of smell. It can smell food from a great distance, far further than we could ever hear or see. For most of the year it roams the forest alone and walks long paths in search of food.

When winter draws near, the bear gets ready for a long rest. Through the autumn it eats its fill, so that it builds up a thick layer of fat. Then it finds a safe den — a cave, a hollow or a shelter under some roots — and there it sleeps through much of the winter. Its heart beats more slowly then, and its body uses little energy.

Mother bears often give birth to their cubs at just this time. Newborn cubs are tiny and helpless. They keep warm beside their mother and drink her milk, until in spring they come out of the den together into the woken forest.

title: The Light in the Storm
body:
On a rocky cape by the sea stood an old lighthouse. In it lived a keeper named Jakob, who lit the great lamp every evening. Its light reached far out over the waves and showed the ships the way past the dangerous rocks.

One wild night a storm broke out like nothing Jakob had ever known. The wind howled, the rain beat against the windows, and the waves crashed against the rocks. In the middle of the darkness, Jakob suddenly saw a small fishing boat struggling with the waves. The people on board could not find the way to the harbour.

Jakob knew what he had to do. All night he stood by the light and made sure it did not go out. Whenever the flame flickered, he built it up again. He was tired and chilled to the bone, but he did not give up.

Toward morning the storm died down. The fishing boat sailed safely into the harbour. The people on board said that, without the lighthouse's light, they would have been lost in the dark night. Jakob smiled and, weary, went off to rest. His light had once again guided someone home.

body:
In Egypt, a land of hot deserts and the mighty river Nile, giant pyramids rise out of the sand into the sky. The most famous and the largest stand near the town of Giza, close to the great city of Cairo. People built them more than four thousand years ago — at a time when there were no machines, no cranes and no trucks.

Up long ramps they slowly hauled them higher and higher, and stacked them carefully one on top of another. For a single such tower they needed thousands of workers and many years of hard work.

The pyramids were the tombs of the pharaohs, the kings of Egypt. The ancient Egyptians believed that a ruler carries on into another world after death, and that he would need his riches there. So they buried him deep inside the pyramid, together with gold and treasures.

title: The Endless Circle of Water
body:
Look into a glass of water. This very same water may once have flowed down a great river, sailed across a wide sea, or even fallen from the sky as a raindrop long, long ago. For the water on Earth never rests — it travels endlessly and returns again. We call this endless journey the water cycle.

It all begins with the sun. Its warm rays heat the water in the seas, lakes and rivers. Part of this water turns from the heat into invisible water vapour, which rises like warm air high into the sky. We call this evaporation.

High up, the air is cold. Because of the cold, the water vapour thickens again into countless tiny droplets. These join together and make up the clouds we see in the sky. When there are too many droplets in a cloud, and they are too heavy to stay in the air, they fall to the ground as rain, snow or hail.

The water then flows back into the streams, rivers and seas. And when the sun warms it again, the whole thing starts over from the beginning. So water travels in an endless circle — the very same water we drink today has been circling the Earth for millions of years.

title: Why the Sky Is Blue
body:
Have you ever wondered why the sky is blue during the day? The answer hides in the sunlight and in the air around us.

Although sunlight seems white to us, it is really made of all the colours of the rainbow, mixed together. When the sun's rays come down from the sky, they travel through the air that wraps around the Earth. In the air there are countless tiny particles, which scatter the light in every direction.

And here is the secret: blue light is scattered far more strongly than the other colours. That is why blue fills the whole sky, and wherever we look, we see blue.

Toward evening, when the sun sinks low, its rays have to travel through much more air. Then the blue is lost, and the red and orange rays reach us instead. That is exactly why the sky at sunset is so beautifully red and gold.

title: The Tireless Engine in Your Chest
body:
Put your hand on the left side of your chest. You will feel a gentle beating. That is your heart, working tirelessly day and night, from the very moment you were born.

The heart is a muscle, about the size of your clenched fist. It is the engine of your body, and its task is very important: it pumps blood all around your body. The heart works like a strong pump. It pushes blood through long, thin tubes that we call blood vessels. These spread out through the whole body, from your head to the tips of your toes.

Why is this so important? Blood is a real delivery service. It supplies every part of the body with the oxygen and the food it needs to live. Without a steady flow of blood, the body could not work at all.

Your heart beats about a hundred times a minute when you are resting. When you run or play, it beats faster, because then it must bring the body more oxygen. That is why it pounds in your chest after a run.

Through a whole day the heart makes tens of thousands of beats, and through a whole life far too many to count. It never takes a rest. So it is only right that we look after it — with exercise, healthy food and plenty of play in the fresh air.

body:
Have you ever wondered why it is hot in summer and cold in winter? The answer is that the year travels through four seasons, which follow every year in the same order: spring, summer, autumn and winter.

In spring nature wakes from its long winter sleep. The trees push out fresh green leaves, the meadows dress themselves in colourful flowers, and the birds return from warm lands to build their nests. Everything is full of new life.

title: Why a Tree Drops Its Leaves
body:
Every autumn something wonderful happens. The leaves on the trees turn from green into fiery red, orange and golden-yellow shades. But why does this happen, and why do the leaves then fall?

Through the summer the leaves are full of green colour. This colour is very important for the tree, because it helps the tree to make its food out of sunlight, water and air. Since there is so much green colour, it covers up all the other colours in the leaf.

When the autumn days grow shorter and it gets cooler, the tree feels that winter is coming. It no longer makes the green colour, and this slowly fades away. Only then do the yellow and red shades show themselves, the ones that were hidden under the green.

The tree drops its leaves for a good reason — so that through the cold winter it can save water and strength. And when the warm sun shines in spring, the bare trees turn green once more.

title: How Bees Survive the Winter
body:
When winter comes and there are no flowers left outside, many people wonder where the bees go. Unlike many insects, bees do not die in winter, and they do not sleep through it either. Instead, they stay together inside their hive.

Through the warm summer the bees busily gathered honey. It is this honey that serves as their stored food in winter. When the cold comes, all the bees squeeze into one big, tight ball, which we call a winter cluster. In the middle of the cluster is their queen.

The bees then begin to move their muscles quickly, and in this way they make warmth, just as we do when we are cold. Because they keep taking turns — first one bee is at the cold edge, then another — not one of them freezes. So it stays warm inside the cluster all winter long, until in spring the first flowers greet them again.

body: Winter is a cold season. Snow falls from the sky. Everything turns white. The trees and roofs are white. The children play in the snow. They make a snowman. Outside it is very cold.

title: Why It Rains
body: Rain is very important for nature. Without it, plants could not grow. Rain forms in the clouds, high up in the sky. In a cloud there are thousands of tiny water droplets. When these droplets join into bigger ones, they become too heavy and fall to the ground. Then we say that it is raining. The rain waters the earth, and the plants are glad of it.

title: Life in the Forest
body: A forest is full of life. In it grow tall trees, bushes, moss and mushrooms. Among the trees and beneath them live thousands of animals. Squirrels leap along the branches and birds sing, beetles crawl over the ground, and in the thickets deer, foxes and stags hide away. The trees in a forest are very important, because they clean the air we breathe. In summer they give us pleasant shade, and to many animals they give a home and food. That is why we must be respectful in the forest: we do not shout, we do not leave litter, and we do not destroy the plants.

title: The River's Journey to the Sea
body:
Every river has its own path, which begins high up in the mountains. There a small spring wells up out of the earth, or the snow melts. Out of these first droplets a little stream is formed, babbling downhill along the slope.

Along the way other streams join it, and it grows bigger and bigger. In time it turns into a wide river. The river flows through valleys and towns, sometimes calmly, and in other places fast and wild. On its way it waters the fields, the forests and the animals, and it gives people water to drink.

Slowly the river draws near to its goal. At last it reaches the sea and pours into it. There its long journey ends — and yet the water travels on, for the sun lifts vapour from the sea again, and somewhere high in the mountains a new river is born.

title: The Wind We Cannot See
body: We cannot see the wind, but we can feel it and hear it. It strokes our face, rocks the branches of the trees, and drives the clouds across the sky. But what actually is the wind? The wind is moving air. Although we cannot see air, it is all around us. When one part of the air warms up and another stays cool, the air begins to move — and we feel this movement as wind. Sometimes the wind is gentle and pleasant; in spring it dries our washing and carries the scent of flowers. At other times it is strong and wild, and breaks the branches. But the wind is useful too: it scatters the seeds of plants and turns the sails of windmills.

title: From a Seed It Grows
body: We plant a small seed in the ground. The seed gets water and sun. From it a little sprout grows. The sprout grows higher and higher. It becomes a big plant. From a seed a flower or a tree can grow.

title: The Wonder of a Snowflake
body: In winter, snowflakes fall from the sky. Each snowflake is made of frozen water. When it is cold enough outside, the tiny droplets in a cloud turn into ice. Snowflakes have six arms, and every single one is different. No two are exactly alike. When many of them fall together, everything turns white.

title: Birds Fly South
body: When autumn draws near, many a bird gets ready for a long journey. A great many birds do not spend the winter here, but fly away to warmer places in the south. We call this migration. The birds fly away because in winter the food runs short here — the insects and seeds that they eat. Some of them fly thousands of kilometres, even over seas and mountains. They often fly together in big flocks, and in this way they help one another. In spring, when it grows warm here again and there is plenty of food, the very same birds come back home.

title: The First Ice on the Puddle
body: When real winter comes, it gets very cold outside. At night the water in puddles and at the edges of lakes turns to ice. This happens because water hardens in the cold. Ice is hard, smooth and slippery. In the morning we can see a thin layer of ice on a puddle. If you step on it, it cracks quietly. But we must be very careful about ice on a lake, because it can be far too thin.
